title: Alaska Packers' Ass'n v. Domenico
lead: After reaching a remote salmon operation, a crew refused the work it had already promised unless its seasonal pay increased. The resulting wage suit turned on unchanged duties, rejected equipment allegations, and whether compelled assent could support a replacement bargain.

actors.name: Alaska Packers’ Association
actors.role: Operator of the Alaska fishing and canning enterprise; employer, admiralty respondent, and appellant.

actors.name: Domenico and fellow workers
actors.role: Sailors and fishermen who sought increased seasonal wages; admiralty libelants and appellees.

actors.name: The superintendent
actors.role: Local company representative who agreed to increased pay after warning that he lacked authority to change the original contracts.

proceedings: Workers sued in admiralty for additional wages; trial court rejected defective-net allegations but entered judgment for workers.
Ninth Circuit assumed authority and formation for analysis, found no consideration, and reversed on May 26, 1902.
Remand directed entry of judgment for the Association with costs.
limits: The defective-net explanation was rejected as fact. The court assumed, but did not decide, superintendent authority and did not independently decide releases. Its actual ground was the pre-existing-duty rule, not later Restatement duress or modification provisions.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with complete effective canonical brief; no new independent full-opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The crew commits to an Alaska season at stated pay
sections.cue: What services were already owed before the dispute?
paragraphs: Domenico and fellow workers agreed in San Francisco to sail to Pyramid Harbor, Alaska, and serve as sailors and fishermen for Alaska Packers’ Association. Their duties included ordinary ship work, loading and unloading, and other work requested by the captain or company agent.

The assigned introduction gives seasonal compensation as $50 plus two cents for each red salmon in whose catching a worker participated. The full opinion also describes later shipping articles specifying $60 plus the same per-fish amount. These source details should remain distinct. In either account, binding agreements fixed compensation before the later demand for $100 for the same season’s services.

The Association had about $150,000 invested in its cannery. Its remote operation depended on a short fishing season. After the crew arrived and began work, replacing it quickly was no longer practicable.

sources.pinpoint: Material facts; C&M pp.470–71; 117 F. at 99–102

sections.title: The workers stop, and the superintendent promises more
sections.cue: Why did his assent not necessarily show the Association voluntarily released its rights?
paragraphs: On May 19, the workers stopped together and demanded $100. They threatened to abandon work and return to San Francisco unless paid more. The superintendent could not obtain replacements in time, so the threat imperiled the operation rather than merely making ordinary rehiring inconvenient.

The superintendent first tried to persuade the crew to resume. On May 22, an agreement was prepared retaining the earlier terms with increased compensation. He expressly told the workers that he lacked authority to alter their original contracts. They nevertheless relied on the resulting promise and completed the work.

When the expedition returned to San Francisco, the Association refused the increase. The full report describes payments and releases under the original arrangements, but the appellate decision did not independently resolve whether those releases defeated recovery. The Association itself had not learned of the refusal to perform until the expedition returned.

sources.pinpoint: Material facts and authority; C&M pp.470–71; 117 F. at 99–105

sections.title: The trial court rejects the asserted equipment problem but awards wages
sections.cue: Which factual premise governed the appeal?
paragraphs: The workers sued in admiralty, where they were called libelants and the Association the respondent. They tried to justify stopping by claiming the fishing nets were rotten or unusable. Because pay partly depended on the catch, genuinely deficient equipment could have changed the employer’s performance and the crew’s obligations.

After conflicting testimony, the trial court rejected that contention. It reasoned that the Association’s investment and own dependence on the catch made knowingly furnishing unusable nets improbable. It nonetheless entered judgment for the workers, reported at 112 F. 554.

The Association appealed. Judge Ross, writing for a Ninth Circuit panel with Judges Gilbert and Hawley, accepted the trial judge’s net finding because that judge had heard and seen the witnesses. He assumed both that the new agreement was made and that the superintendent had authority, then asked whether consideration supported it. That sufficient legal issue left actual authority undecided.

sources.pinpoint: Trial and appellate posture; C&M pp.470–71; 117 F. at 99–105

sections.title: Ross finds no new performance supporting the higher promise
sections.cue: Why was practical value to the employer insufficient?
paragraphs: The crew knowingly owed the specified Alaska services for agreed pay. The new promise required no additional work, longer season, new responsibility, or surrender of a genuine disputed claim. It asked for precisely the performance already due. Avoiding disruption had obvious practical value to the Association, but did not supply a newly bargained-for legal benefit under the rule applied.

The rejected net contention mattered: consideration analysis proceeded on an unjustified refusal to perform, not a finding that the employer had disabled performance. Accepting the allegation as fact would produce a different case. Performing an existing duty therefore supplied no consideration for the additional wage promise.

sources.pinpoint: Consideration reasoning; C&M pp.471–73; 117 F. at 102–05

sections.title: The same circumstances defeat rescission, waiver, and estoppel
sections.cue: Why did completion of the season not cure the defect?
paragraphs: The demand came after capital was committed, during a narrow season, and when replacement labor was unavailable. Ross treated that leverage as exploitation of dependence on promised work, not a fresh exchange freely selected by both parties. The superintendent’s express authority disclaimer further weakened any inference that the Association knowingly abandoned its original rights. The record did not support voluntary rescission and substitution or waiver merely from his apparent assent.

The court used King v. Railway Co. to reject estoppel based on eventually completing the work. A worker who extracts an additional promise by unjustifiably refusing an existing obligation cannot turn later performance of that obligation into protected reliance barring the consideration defense. Otherwise the worker’s own breach would create the foundation for enforcement.

Quoted reasoning from Lingenfelder v. Brewing Co., involving an architect demanding more for already-promised services, reinforced the point. Calling the arrangement a new contract did not identify new performance. These were supporting authorities, not separate opinions in this case. The concern was opportunistic refusal under these facts, not judicial permission to adjust every bargain the court thought underpriced.

sources.pinpoint: Rescission, waiver, and estoppel; C&M pp.471–73

sections.title: The Association wins judgment, while later reforms pose different questions
paragraphs: On May 26, 1902, the Ninth Circuit reversed and remanded with directions to enter judgment for the Association with costs. The crew could not recover the asserted increase. No separate concurrence or dissent appeared. Lack of consideration was the operative ground; coercive circumstances explained why apparent assent and completed work did not establish a voluntary replacement or protected reliance.

Later Restatement § 89 can support some modifications without new consideration, but replacement difficulty alone does not establish unforeseen circumstances supporting a fair adjustment, and § 89(c) does not automatically protect every performance of an existing duty. New York General Obligations Law § 5-1103 can remove consideration objections to qualifying signed modifications without supplying authority or eliminating duress. Uniform Commercial Code § 2-209 applies to goods modifications; a crew’s services contract is not a goods sale merely because its employer sells salmon.

Those are later-law comparisons, not this court’s holdings or applications of later Restatement §§ 175–176. Proven defective equipment, additional services, a genuinely disputed duty, or a voluntary fair adjustment might change the analysis, but those counterfactuals were not established here. The source does not report further collection or payment proceedings.

sources.pinpoint: Judgment and later-law notes; 117 F. at 105; C&M pp.473–77
